title: Latency-bound burst escrow and tenant throttle proposal
content:
Purpose

This doc sketches a proposal for a latency-aware burst escrow and tenant throttling system for Dedicated capacity. Goal: let customers safely consume short-term extra capacity while preserving tail latency SLOs for paying tenants and preventing noisy neighbor impact. This is a working draft — experiment-first, ops-heavy at launch.

Problem statement

- We see recurring short spikes (microbursts) where tenant demand temporarily exceeds their committed capacity, causing: higher p95/p99, request queueing, and evictions in overloaded slices.
- Existing soft-burst approaches (simple credits) struggle to protect latency SLOs when multiple tenants burst simultaneously or when bursts persist slightly longer than expected.
- Need a mechanism that: 1) grants controlled short-term capacity with explicit accounting, 2) enforces latency envelopes per latency-class, 3) degrades tenants in a predictable, observable way rather than opaque throttles.

High-level concept

- Burst escrow: each tenant can draw from an escrow balance (seconds of vGPU time equivalent) when below a latency budget. Escrow is funded by commitments, credits, or on-demand purchase.
- Latency guardrail: transient extra capacity is only granted when the system-wide latency headroom for the target latency class (e.g., p95 < SLO threshold) is available. If headroom is low, grants are curtailed automatically.
- Throttle hierarchy: when overall headroom is exhausted, apply a tiered throttle rather than immediate rejection: 1) soft-rate-limit (token-bucket slowdown), 2) degrade to cheaper model variants or lower precision (if configured), 3) hard reject.
- Escrow reclaim and repayment: if a tenant uses escrow and system remains healthy, usage is billed immediately (or charged to credits). If system enters stress, in-flight escrow can be partially reclaimed via slow-down signals and queued fallback routing.

Key design components

1) Metrics and signals
- Per-host and per-pool latency SLO telemetry: rolling p50/p95/p99 for critical routes.
- Demand signal: instantaneous request concurrency, token/operation weight, and queued length.
- Escrow balance per-tenant: available credits, recent draw-rate, repayment schedule.
- Effective headroom metric: computed as (SLO threshold - current p95) normalized by capacity curve; includes margin for safety.

2) Grant algorithm (fast path)
- When a request arrives: check tenant allocated capacity + current concurrent usage. If below commit -> serve normally.
- If over commit but escrow_balance > 0 -> evaluate pool headroom.
- If headroom >= grant_threshold -> allow grant sized proportional to min(escrow_balance, max_burst_size_for_latency_class).
- Grants are tokenized: a small time-limited grant (e.g., up to 10s of prefix compute). Each grant reduces escrow balance.
- Grants are optimistic and revocable: control plane keeps a cheap lease to revoke grants if headroom collapses.

3) Latency guardrail and revocation
- Periodic headroom assessor (100ms cadence) computes headroom per pool & latency class.
- On headroom drop below safe_margin -> start revocation wave: stop issuing new grants, and attempt to revoke existing grants by returning a short-lived HTTP/GRPC 'slowdown' response header that instructs SDK to backoff (client-side cooperative). If client does not reduce, server starts to throttle.

4) Tiered throttle policy
- Soft rate-limit: per-route adjustable token-bucket that reduces allowed QPS gradually.
- Model fallback: server-side reroute to configured fallback model instance (quantized or smaller). Fallback only used when tenant opted-in or a policy exists.
- Hard reject: reject with clear error code and reason, include diagnostics for retry-after and escrow state.

5) Billing and economics
- Escrow usage recorded at grant time; two modes: charged-on-use or post-facto invoice for committed-reserve customers.
- Discounted microburst SKU for committed tenants: lower per-unit cost for escrow draws under X seconds/day.
- Overflow marketplace: optionally allow on-demand buys from pooled spare capacity at higher rate (subject to headroom check).

Operational interactions and UI

- Console: show live escrow balance, recent draws, and predicted safe burst window (seconds) per time-of-day.
- Alerts: Notify when tenant enters sustained escrow drain (>Y% of balance in Z mins), and when revocation events occur impacting a tenant.
- Audit logs: Every grant/ revoke/ fallback must log request ids, pool ids, and headroom snapshot.

Runbook excerpts (ops-friendly)

- If pool p95 spikes and >SLO: 1) identify top 5 tenants by recent grants, 2) temporarily pause escrow grants for non-enterprise tiers, 3) enable admission control to throttle new requests to protected lanes.
- Emergency rollback: rollback grant allocator config to strict mode (no escrow) via feature flag.
- Post-incident: run cost/slo reconciliation to see if escrow draws correlated with billing disputes.

Safety and fairness considerations

- Fair-share in contention: when multiple tenants request escrow and headroom is tight, prefer tenants with higher commit tiers or those with low recent usage (avoid starving small bursty tenants forever). Keep a lottery-weighted fairness fallback.
- Prevent gaming: decay escrow refunds for artificially fragmented requests (very short-lived repeated grants). Add smoothing window to indictment grants.
- Isolation-by-class: separate headroom for latency-sensitive (chat completions) vs batch (embeddings) workloads. Do not let embeddings bursts consume chat headroom.

APIs and config knobs (product-facing)

- Tenant config: escrow_enabled (bool), max_burst_seconds, fallback_model_alias, burst_tier (on-demand | committed-discount | none), throttle_policy_id.
- Admin API: pool-level headroom_margin, grant_window_size, revocation_grace_ms, on_demand_price_multiplier.
- Telemetry endpoints: /v1/escrow/usage, /v1/escrow/balance, /v1/escrow/grants (recent).

Implementation notes (engineering pointers)

- Fast path at serving runtime: grants must be cheap 2-3 memops. Represent grants as ephemeral tokens validated by local runtime; central control plane publishes headroom summaries to edge caches.
- Use continuous batching awareness: grants include estimated token cost; scheduler batches only up to headroom scaled tokens.
- Fallback routing: maintain warm fallback model pools to avoid cold-start latency when falling back.

Open questions (short list)

- Pricing model: immediate per-second billing vs aggregated daily invoice — which minimizes disputes and simplifies rollbacks? (
- Client behavior: how many SDKs will honor server 'slowdown' header? Do we need server-side enforcement regardless?
- Revocation UX: best way to surface partial revokes to long-running streaming responses? Graceful degrade of output vs cutting stream.
- Simulation: what synthetic workload mix should we use to simulate multi-tenant concurrent bursts?

Next steps and timeline (proposal)

- 2 weeks: prototype headroom estimator + simple grant token at dev cluster (engineers: Carlos, Priya).
- 3 weeks: simulation harness (SRE + applied-ml) to run multi-tenant burst scenarios and measure p95/p99 impact.
- 2 weeks: integrate simple console view + telemetry hooks.
- 4 weeks: limited dogfood with internal tenants, opt-in by teams, gather metrics and iterate.
- Go/no-go gating: must show p95 improvement vs naive credit model under 95th percentile of mixed-burst tests. Also require clear audit trail.

Notes to reviewers

- This is intentionally conservative on revocation: prefer degrading experience predictably over sudden failures. We expect several iterations.
- Please call out specific edge cases in the open questions section or add suggested simulation scenarios in the linked JIRA DED-4821.

Raw sketches and references
